newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico tension rises as government warns rebels.
newsitem.headline: Mexico tension rises as government warns rebels.

text.p: The Mexican government issued on Friday its sternest warning this year to Zapatista Indian rebels, telling them they risked arrest and an end to peace talks if they left their jungle hideouts to make a rumoured journey to Mexico City.
Chief official negotiator Marcos Bernal told the Zapatistas they would be breaking the law if they moved outside their home state of Chiapas while talks were stalled.

"If the law is broken, we return to a previous legal status of the Zapatistas, where they are a group that has declared war on the Mexican government, that is clandestine and posseses illegal weapons. That implies a lot of crimes," Bernal told Mexico City's Radio Red.
Long-running peace talks between the two sides were suspended in early September after the Zapatistas accused the government of acting in bad faith.
Tension rose sharply this week after organisers of an Indian rights forum in Mexico City said top Zapatista commanders had accepted their invitation to attend next week.

Organisers of the forum said they expected Zapatista leaders to travel at the weekend but Javier Elorriaga, one of the rebels' top civilian representatives, told Reuters the rebel leaders would wait until next week.

The government has already been shaken by the appearance of a new and more violent Marxist guerrilla group in June, the Marxist Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR). A propaganda battle against popular Zapatista leaders who might appear in central Mexico City has put the government under further pressure.

President Ernesto Zedillo appealed to the Zapatistas on a visit to Chiapas on Thursday to return to peace negotiations. He warned them against letting "outside interests, motivated by protagonistic desires" interfere with what he called a "genuine will to have dialogue."
The Zapatista leadership has not yet made clear whether top commanders will in fact travel to Mexico City next week.
Elorriaga told Reuters the Zapatistas were still considering whether or not to make their first break out of the jungle since their uprising in January 1994.
"The threats (against them) are very strong, we don't want to expose them and they can't come out firing either," he said.

Elorriaga said a commission of left-wing "notables" would travel to the Chiapas jungle on Monday to meet the commanders and take a decision about the journey. In the meantime, he alleged, troops in the area were being reinforced.
"The military pressure is very strong," he said. "It is confirmed that (various Zapatista commanders) want to come to the Indian Congress but what is not confirmed is if they are able to."

Bernal said if the rebels did leave Chiapas they would be violating the terms of a special peace law passed in March 1995 which suspended arrest warrants against the Zapatista leaders to allow negotiations.
The government would then act to carry out the arrest warrants against 15 commanders, including the charismatic rebel chief Subcommander Marcos, he added.
